title: Frustration and boundaries
description: Teacher-shared phrases for annoyance, frustration, asking for space, and setting boundaries.
source: Learner-provided lesson note shared as a WhatsApp image.

cards.translation: Say it in Spanish; match the speaker’s gender.
cards.note: Use harto for a man and harta for a woman.

cards.translation: Say it to one person informally.
answers: me estas poniendo de los nervios
cards.answer: Me estás poniendo de los nervios.
cards.note: Ponerse de los nervios means to become very irritated or nervous.

cards.translation: Say it about a person; match their gender.
cards.note: Pesado describes an annoying person; its ending agrees with that person.

cards.translation: Say it to one person informally.
cards.note: Déjame en paz is direct and means leave me in peace.

cards.translation: Say it to one person informally.
cards.note: This negative tú command uses the present subjunctive form molestes.

cards.translation: Say it firmly in Spanish.
cards.note: Ya basta and basta ya both mean enough already.

cards.translation: Use the informal idiom with narices.
cards.note: Literally up to the nose, this means being completely fed up.

cards.translation: Say it in Spanish.
cards.note: Aguantar means to endure or put up with something.

cards.translation: Say it to one person; match the speaker’s gender.
cards.note: The ending of harto or harta agrees with the speaker, not the listener.

cards.translation: Use the short expression with rabia.
cards.note: Qué rabia expresses frustration or annoyance.

cards.translation: Use the idiom with quicio.
cards.note: Sacar de quicio means to drive someone up the wall.

cards.translation: Say it in Spanish.
cards.note: Estar + gerund expresses an action in progress.

cards.prompt: It puts me in a bad mood.
cards.translation: Say it in Spanish.
cards.note: Poner de mal humor means to put someone in a bad mood.

cards.prompt: I have no patience for this.
cards.translation: Say it in Spanish.
cards.note: Tener paciencia means to have patience.

cards.translation: Use the short expression with fastidio.
cards.note: Fastidio means annoyance, bother, or nuisance.

cards.translation: Use the strong informal expression common in Spain.
cards.note: This is informal and somewhat crude; avoid it in polite or professional settings.

cards.translation: Use the expression with venir and eso.
cards.note: Literally do not come to me with that, this rejects an excuse or argument.

cards.translation: Say it to one person informally.
cards.note: Déjalo ya means stop it or leave it now.

cards.translation: Say it to one person informally.
cards.note: Enfadar is common in Spain; enojar is common in much of Latin America.

cards.prompt: I need to clear my head.
cards.translation: Say it in Spanish.
cards.note: Despejarse means to clear one’s head or get some mental space.
